 1 I.       INTRODUCTION

 2          In its third attempt to state a claim, and with the benefit of extensive expedited discovery

 3 and briefing on its motion for a preliminary injunction, Apple has still failed to plead a single alleged

 4 trade secret as required by the governing pleading standards. Instead of improving its trade secret

 5 identification, Apple merely adds a new defendant, Dr. Zijing Zeng, asserting threadbare allegations

 6 against him based on transparent misrepresentations of fact. Because documents cited by the SAC

 7 are inconsistent with those misrepresentations, those allegations should be disregarded.

 8          Apple’s SAC should thus be dismissed on two grounds. First, the SAC’s trade secret

 9 misappropriation claim should be dismissed as to OPPO and Dr. Zeng because it fails to adequately

10 allege the trade secrets supposedly at issue. Like its previous attempts, Apple continues to offer

11 only generic categories of alleged trade secrets seemingly covering entire areas of smartwatch

12 technology, such as “design information for health sensing technology,” without identifying what

13 specific information within those broad categories Apple claims is entitled to trade secret protection.

14 Under black-letter law, that is not enough to state a claim. Apple’s failure to identify its trade

15 secrets, especially after obtaining early and extensive discovery, is fatal. Second, the claim should

16 also be dismissed as to Dr. Zeng because it fails to adequately allege misappropriation. Apple’s

17 claim against Dr. Zeng is, fundamentally, that Dr. Zeng improperly induced Dr. Shi to obtain,

18 disclose, or use Apple’s purported trade secrets. But the facts alleged in the SAC, when disentangled

19 from Apple’s selective quotations and conclusory editorializing, do not support such a claim. The

20 facts are far more mundane, reflecting nothing more than standard employee recruitment. Because

21 Apple fails to plausibly allege any misappropriation by Dr. Zeng, the claim against him should be

22 dismissed for that independent reason.

23          Lastly, because Apple has now had three attempts to allege plausible claims, Apple’s sole

24 claim against OPPO and Dr. Zeng should be dismissed with prejudice.

 9 IV.      ARGUMENT

10          To state a claim for trade secret misappropriation under the DTSA, “a plaintiff must allege

11 (1) that it is the owner of a trade secret; (2) that the defendant misappropriated the trade secret; and

12 (3) that it was damaged by the defendant’s actions.” Navigation Holdings, LLC v. Molavi, 445 F.

13 Supp. 3d 69, 78 (N.D. Cal. 2020).

14          A.      Apple Fails to Adequately Allege the Trade Secrets at Issue

15          Apple’s SAC fails at the threshold because it fails to allege that Apple owns any protectable

16 trade secrets. “A true trade secret plaintiff ought to be able to identify, up front, and with specificity

17 the particulars of the trade secrets without any discovery.” Jobscience, Inc. v. CVPartners, Inc.,

18 2014 WL 852477, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 28, 2014); see also Trustwell v. RLH Assets, LLC, 2025 WL

19 2697107, at *5 (D. Or. Sept. 22, 2025) (“Allegations that set out purported trade secrets in broad,

20 categorical terms that are merely descriptive of the types of information that generally may qualify

21 as protectable trade secrets are insufficient to state a claim.”) (internal quotations and citations

22 omitted); Quintara Biosciences, Inc. v. Ruifeng Biztech, Inc., 149 F.4th 1081, 1088 (9th Cir. 2025)

23 (holding that, even based on “the conventional procedures under the Federal Rules of Civil

24 Procedure,” a trade secret plaintiff must “identify a trade secret with sufficient particularity” and not

 3          Despite this clear requirement, it has long been recognized that trade secret plaintiffs

 4 virtually never “provide a precise and complete identification of the alleged trade secrets at issue

 5 without a court order requiring them to do so.” Charles Tait Graves & Brian D. Range, Identification

 6 of Trade Secret Claims in Litigation: Solutions for a Ubiquitous Dispute, 5 Nw. J. Tech. Intell. Prop.

 7 68, 68 (2006). “This is a strategy, not an accident.” Id.; see also JobScience, 2014 WL 852477 at

 8 *5 (describing the “old trick of vague pleading with the blanks to be filled in only after discovery”).

 9 It is an effective strategy because, unless courts require plaintiffs to plead trade secrets with the

10 particularity required by law, “it is easy to allege theft of trade secrets with vagueness, then take

11 discovery into the defendants’ files, and then cleverly specify what ever happens to be there as

12 having been trade secrets stolen from plaintiff.” Id.

13          Courts routinely dismiss trade secret claims where the complaint does not identify the

14 alleged trade secrets with sufficient particularity to put the defendants on notice of which trade

15 secrets they allegedly misappropriated. Lamont v. Conner, 2019 WL 1369928, at *8 (N.D. Cal.

16 Mar. 26, 2019) (granting motion to dismiss where “Plaintiff’s description of his trade secrets as

17 stated in the complaint are not plead with sufficient particularity”); AlterG, Inc. v. Boost Treadmills

18 LLC, 388 F. Supp. 3d 1133, 1144 (N.D. Cal. 2019) (granting motion to dismiss where plaintiff

19 “fail[ed] to identify its allegedly misappropriated trade secrets with sufficient particularity to state

20 a claim under the DTSA”); Vendavo, Inc. v. Price f(x) AG, 2018 WL 1456697 at *4 (N.D. Cal. Mar.

10 presentation “appear[] to have been copied from misappropriated Apple trade secrets,” ¶96, Apple

11 fails to allege that Dr. Zeng had any knowledge of those portions at all, let alone whether those

12 portions might contain protected information. As noted above, to adequately allege an indirect

13 misappropriation theory, Apple must allege that Dr. Zeng “knew or had reason to know” that the

14 information was a trade secret. Navigation Holdings, LLC, 445 F. Supp. 3d at 79. The SAC fails

15 to do so as to the July 16 presentation.

16          With regard to the August 1 presentation, Apple alleges that “Dr. Zeng arranged for Dr. Shi

17 to give a detailed presentation” to employees, and that “[a]t Dr. Zeng’s request, Dr. Shi shared

24 Zeng believed there to be trade-secret information in Dr. Shi’s possession. But, again, no such facts

 4          This Court has discretion to deny leave to amend. See, e.g., Salameh v. Tarsadia Hotel, 726

 8 by amendment.” Salameh, 726 F.3d at 1133 (internal quotations and citations omitted). Where the

 9 plaintiff has already had an opportunity to amend and to conduct even “minimal discovery,”

10         categorical terms, more descriptive of the types of information that generally may qualify

12         has a basis to believe actually were misappropriated here.”); Synopsys, Inc. v. ATopTech,

23         Zeng. Even if Apple had adequately identified trade secrets and their disclosure by Dr.
